newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Random violence haunts luckless Albania.
newsitem.headline: Random violence haunts luckless Albania.

text.p: Protests and random violence hit Albania again on Thursday amid fears that more get-rich-quick investment schemes could collapse and plunge the Balkan country further into crisis.
Western governments expressed concern, warning nationals to be careful. They also discussed ways to help Europe's poorest state and head off a possible new wave of mass immigration.
Italy advised its nationals to consider restricting travel within and to Albania over the next few days, following recent bloody riots and anti-government protests.
France, voicing "extreme concern", said the European Union was discussing ways of helping end the crisis through dialogue between the right-wing government and the opposition.

Police cordoned off Tirana's Skanderbeg Square on Thursday to prevent anti-government demonstrations but protesters took to the streets for a ninth day in the southern seaside town of Vlore to demand reimbursement for lost funds.
Several thousand demonstrators chanted "Give us our money" and "Resign, resign", blaming the government for letting the schemes flourish for the past five years.
Vlore has been hit by a wave of violence since police were stoned, stripped and forced to leave the town earlier this week in clashes which left three people dead.

A policeman was shot dead on Wednesday, another officer's house was attacked and an 18-year-old girl was abducted by masked men from her parents' home, apparently to be sold to a prostitution ring, police said.

In Tirana, several men seized the car of the opposition Socialist Party Secretary General, Rexhep Mejdani, on Thursday, drove it to a village and dumped it off a cliff. Mejdani was not in the car when it was seized in central Tirana.
Europe's poorhouse, emerging from 40 years of isolation and Stalinist rule in 1990, Albania has been rocked by a month of protests after several dubious investment schemes collapsed.

Hundreds of thousands of Albanians from all walks of life lost their life savings in the popular "pyramid" schemes, which often used money from new investors to cover high yield returns for earlier investors.

Diplomats and officials have said much of the money pumped into the schemes came from illegal trade in refugees and drugs as well as illegal Albanian workers in EU countries, who sent their earnings home to relatives.

But doctors, lawyers, government officials and average Albanians also poured money into the schemes, thought to have total investments of some $2 billion -- a sum equal roughly to Albania's annual gross domestic product.

The failed Vlore scheme alone was estimated to have had investments of $500 million. The government has frozen assets of two other schemes totalling $300 million and is paying out a percentage of that to luckless investors.
Prime Minister Alexander Meksi said on Thursday that the government could do no more than hand out the money which it had frozen.
A long queue of people formed outside the failed Populli scheme in Tirana on Thursday, waiting for a truck to deliver another load of cash and a 60 percent reimbursement.

Asked if the government would cover losses, Meksi said: "No. We are distributing the money we have managed to freeze in the banks. That's all we can do. It would be nonsense for us to try to take the place of the failed schemes."

In the interview published in Italy's Corriere della Sera newspaper, he said the government was also trying to establish what chance schemes which were still afloat had of returning money to investors.
"We have advised them to give everything back, as soon as possible. And if they want to carry on, to change their method," he said.
Meksi denied that either he or President Sali Berisha were involved in the schemes, saying such accusations were aimed at stirring up anti-government crowds.

"It's a good way of heating up the crowd. They've also said it about me. The only money I have belongs to the government and I can't go handing out government money which belongs to all the people of Albania," he said.
